title: QCAT Practice Direction No 10 of 2025 — Accuracy of References in Submissions
description: QCAT practice direction requiring a named responsible person for written and oral submissions and personal verification of all references, with referral to the Legal Services Commissioner for non-existent citations.
content: Signed by the Hon Justice Kerri Mellifont, President, on 17 October 2025, this Practice Direction mirrors Supreme Court of Queensland Practice Direction 5 of 2025. Rather than regulating generative AI use directly, it targets the risk of inaccurate or fictitious references reaching the Tribunal. It records that generative AI tools may produce coherent and plausible responses that are inaccurate or fictitious, including references to non-existent case authorities, legislative references and legal and academic resources, and that a further risk arises where generative AI is used to formulate or reformulate the expression of a submission without the result being sufficiently checked. For written submissions, the person or persons taking responsibility for the contents — the responsible person — must be identified by name at the end of the document; where that person is a legal practitioner it must be the individual solicitor or barrister, and naming the firm on the record is not sufficient. For oral submissions the responsible person is the person making them, who thereby also becomes a responsible person for the written submissions. A legal practitioner who is a responsible person must verify the accuracy and relevance of any references to legislation, authorities or other sources, and ensure the submission is expressed in terms reflecting their judgment as to the proper discharge of their professional and ethical obligations. Placing their name on a written submission, or advancing oral submissions, is an implied representation to the Tribunal that they have done so. The Practice Direction ties those duties to rules 12, 25, 26, 37, 41 and 57 of the Barristers' Conduct Rules and rules 3, 4, 5, 17, 19 and 37 of the Solicitors' Conduct Rules. Practitioners responsible for submissions found to contain references to non-existent cases, legislation or other material may be referred to the Legal Services Commissioner for investigation and may be required to show cause why a personal costs order should not be made against them. Self-represented litigants are directed to the Queensland Courts guidelines for non-lawyers, updated 15 September 2025. The Practice Direction will be reviewed regularly.

title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — Guidelines for Responsible Use by Non-Lawyers
description: Queensland Courts plain-language guidelines for self-represented litigants and other non-lawyers using generative AI in civil and criminal proceedings.
content: These Guidelines apply to civil and criminal proceedings in Queensland courts and tribunals, including the Supreme Court, District Court and Planning and Environment Court, and are directed to people who are not lawyers. They are the litigant-facing counterpart to the Queensland Courts guidelines for judicial officers and to the Accuracy of References in Submissions practice directions issued across the Queensland court and tribunal hierarchy; QCAT Practice Direction No 10 of 2025 directs self-represented litigants to read them and records that they were updated on 15 September 2025. The Guidelines explain in plain language what generative AI chatbots are and what they can usefully do, including summarising material, changing tone or format, generating new text or a plan for new text in a specific format, and answering questions on a topic. They emphasise that these tools can get information wrong, that AI-generated content should never be assumed to be correct, and that a person who puts material before a court remains responsible for its accuracy whether or not generative AI helped produce it. They address the risk of fabricated cases, citations and legislative references, the need to check anything a chatbot produces against an authoritative source before relying on it, and the privacy and confidentiality risks of entering personal or case information into publicly available tools. The document prints the date 15 September 2025 and a version history recording 'Guideline issued on 13 May 2024' and 'Revised version issued on 15 September 2025'; QCAT Practice Direction No 10 of 2025 likewise cites the Guidelines as 'updated 15 September 2025'.

title: The Use of Generative AI — Guidelines for Judicial Officers
description: Queensland Courts guidelines governing judicial officers' and their staff's use of generative AI, revised on 15 September 2025.
content: First issued on 13 May 2024 and reissued in a revised version on 15 September 2025, these Guidelines govern the use of generative AI by Queensland judicial officers and their staff. They open with the principle that any use of generative AI tools by judicial officers and their staff must be consistent with the fulfilment of the judiciary's obligation to do equal justice to all persons according to law. They address what generative AI is and how it fails, the confidentiality of court information and the risks of entering it into publicly available tools, and the limits on relying on generative AI output in the exercise of the judicial function, including in the preparation of reasons. The revised version also addresses the intersection with expert evidence: it directs judicial officers to consider whether generative AI has been used in the formulation or expression of an opinion contained in an expert report, and whether the expert should be required to identify in their report the precise way in which they have used AI. That provision sits alongside Supreme Court of Queensland Practice Direction Number 14 of 2024 on expert evidence in criminal proceedings, which was amended and reissued on 10 September 2025 to add generative AI requirements for experts. The Guidelines are the bench-facing counterpart to the Queensland Courts guidelines for non-lawyers and to the Accuracy of References in Submissions practice directions issued across the Queensland hierarchy. A version history at the end of the document records both the original issue on 13 May 2024 and the revision on 15 September 2025.

content: Practice Direction Number 14 of 2024 was originally issued on 15 April 2024 and commenced on 15 July 2024, applying to proceedings commenced by an indictment presented on or after that date. It was amended and reissued by Chief Justice H Bowskill on 10 September 2025. The Practice Direction governs expert evidence in criminal proceedings in the Supreme Court of Queensland other than sentences, setting out the form and content required of expert reports and the duties of experts to the Court. The 2025 amendment is the reason the instrument appears in AI guidance registers: subparagraph 16(l) introduces a requirement addressing the use of generative artificial intelligence in the formulation or expression of an opinion contained in an expert report. The Practice Direction includes a transition provision — where an opinion in a report was finalised before the amendment took effect, the expert should furnish a supplementary report addressing the requirements of subparagraph 16(l) to the extent they are able to do so. The instrument is not primarily an AI practice direction; its AI provisions are one component of a broader expert evidence regime, and it is included in the register because it imposes operative generative AI obligations on expert witnesses in Queensland criminal proceedings. It complements the Queensland Courts guidelines for judicial officers, revised on 15 September 2025, which direct judicial officers to consider whether generative AI has been used in an expert opinion. A version history at the end of the document records the original issue on 15 April 2024 and the amendment and reissue on 10 September 2025.

title: Guidelines for the use of generative AI
description: Supreme Court of Western Australia guidelines on generative AI in proceedings, addressed to lawyers, non-lawyers, self-represented litigants and expert witnesses.
content: These Guidelines concern the use of artificial intelligence in proceedings before the Supreme Court of Western Australia and are expressly intended to assist all those involved in proceedings, including lawyers, non-lawyers, self-represented litigants in civil and criminal proceedings, and expert witnesses. They explain that generative AI does not think or reason but predicts word sequences based on training data, that output quality depends entirely on the extent and quality of input data, and that AI-generated content should never be presumed correct and is not a substitute for legal research or human experience and oversight. They warn that publicly available generative AI tools often store and reuse prompts, outputs and data, that the privacy and confidentiality of information provided to such tools may not be guaranteed, and that users should consider what ongoing or future use a tool may make of information before providing it. Paragraph 5 lists the risks: outdated information arising from fixed training cut-off dates; incompleteness, where AI-generated content omits relevant arguments or overlooks essential points; inaccuracy and fabrication, where tools invent cases, authorities or facts and present them confidently as true; jurisdiction issues, where tools draw on jurisdictions with different substantive laws or procedural requirements; and bias, including over- or under-representation of demographics and an inability to understand specific cultural or emotional needs. The principles for use require litigants and practitioners to understand the capabilities and limitations of any tool they use, and to take responsibility for AI-generated content relied on in proceedings. The Guidelines provide that, when directed by the court or where otherwise necessary or appropriate, the use of generative AI in Supreme Court proceedings, including in the preparation of any materials, should be disclosed to other parties and the court. title: Guidelines for New South Wales Judges in respect of Use of Generative AI
description: Guidelines issued by the Chief Justice of New South Wales on 21 November 2024, developed with Heads of Jurisdiction, governing how judges of all NSW courts may and may not use generative AI.
agencies: Supreme Court of New South Wales
content: The Guidelines for New South Wales Judges in respect of Use of Generative AI apply to all courts in New South Wales and were developed after consultation with Heads of Jurisdiction and review of guidelines from other common law courts (para 1). They define Gen AI and give examples of generic and legal-specific large language model programs (paras 2–3). Judges should not use Gen AI in formulating reasons for judgment or in assessing or analysing evidence preparatory to delivering reasons (para 4), and Gen AI should not be used to edit or proof draft judgments; no part of a draft judgment may be submitted to a Gen AI program (para 5). If Gen AI is used for secondary legal research or other purposes, judges must understand its limits, including hallucinated citations, incomplete or non-Australian data, bias, retention of prompts, confidentiality risks, copyright and the risk of granting device permissions (para 6). All Gen AI research output must be closely scrutinised and verified for accuracy, completeness, currency and suitability, and must not substitute for personal research (para 7). Judges should require associates, tipstaves and researchers to disclose any Gen AI use and to verify output separately (para 8). Judges may require litigants and legal representatives to disclose Gen AI use in written submissions and to give an assurance of verification, including for compliance with Practice Note SC Gen 23 (para 9), and should be astute to identify undisclosed use (para 10). Paragraph 11 lists red flags such as non-existent citations, out-of-date or inapplicable case law, obvious substantive errors, repetitive language and foreign spelling. The guidelines will be reviewed regularly (para 12). The Land and Environment Court applies them to its Judges, Commissioners, Acting Commissioners and Registrars.

title: Guidelines: The Use of Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers (County Court of Victoria)
description: County Court of Victoria guidelines, created 5 June 2026 and authorised by Chief Judge Chambers, setting the parameters for the use of artificial intelligence by the Court's judges and judicial registrars.
content: The Guidelines outline the parameters around the use of Artificial Intelligence by Judicial Officers of the County Court of Victoria, defined as Judges and Judicial Registrars of the Court, including Reserve Judges. They were issued alongside Practice Note PNCCV 1-2026 on the use of AI by Court users, which lists them as a related document, and closely mirror the Supreme Court of Victoria's guidelines of 14 May 2026. The Guidelines state they were informed by the eight principles formulated by the Victorian Law Reform Commission to guide the safe use of AI in courts and tribunals. They define AI as a machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions, and distinguish generative AI, public AI (openly accessible tools trained on broad, often public datasets) and closed AI (tools kept within a controlled environment with confidentiality protections). The operative rules provide that Judicial Officers must not use GenAI for judicial decision-making; they consider each matter, exercise their own judgment to reach a decision and give reasons where appropriate. This does not prevent supportive uses of AI by Judicial Officers or Court staff, such as organising and locating case materials, producing summaries and chronologies, assisting legal research and proof-reading, provided these are not a substitute for reading or listening to evidence and submissions or for fact-finding. For case-related matters, Judicial Officers and Court staff must only use AI tools approved by the Court, with approval given having regard to confidentiality and amelioration of other risks. Judicial Officers should give staff clear directions on appropriate AI use and the level of disclosure required. The Guidelines are to be reviewed as technology and the Court's experience change.
aiSummary: County Court of Victoria judicial officers must not use generative AI for judicial decision-making and may use only Court-approved tools for supportive tasks such as summaries, chronologies, research and proof-reading.

title: Litigants in Person Practice Note (GPN-LIP)
description: Federal Court of Australia general practice note for litigants in person, issued by Chief Justice Mortimer on 5 March 2026, which at paragraphs 2.8 to 2.11 directs self-represented litigants on when they may and may not use generative AI programs.
content: GPN-LIP is a General Practice Note of the Federal Court of Australia written in plain language for litigants in person, that is, parties who have a legal case in the Court without a lawyer. It is issued under the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) and litigants are asked to sign an acknowledgement form confirming they have read it. Its generative AI provisions sit in Part 2 (Getting legal help). Paragraph 2.8 directs litigants not to use generative AI programs such as ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini to obtain legal help about whether they have a case they can win, because such programs are not reliable, are not trained like lawyers, may give answers based on American law and can give false answers to legal questions. Paragraph 2.9 similarly warns against social media and pseudolaw sites, noting a litigant can be in serious trouble for making arguments not based on real law. Paragraph 2.10 permits litigants who start or defend a case based on real law and evidence to use AI programs to help explain their case to the Court, but requires them to tell the Court they have done so if asked, to check that all facts from AI programs are correct and complete and that the law is correct, preferably with a lawyer or otherwise using the free legal research databases listed in Attachment D, and warns of serious consequences for giving the Court false information about facts or law. Paragraph 2.11 states the Court will soon publish more about what litigants can and cannot do with AI programs in their cases; that further guidance was issued as GPN-AI on 16 April 2026. The remainder of the practice note covers interpreters, the Court's expectations of litigants in person, the registry, hearings and costs, and includes four attachments on definitions, sections 37M and 37N of the Act, other practice notes and legal research databases.

title: Information for self-represented litigants regarding the use of Generative artificial intelligence in litigation
description: South Australian courts information sheet supplementing the Supreme Court's Generative AI Guidelines, explaining to self-represented litigants the restrictions on uploading litigation documents to AI tools and the need to verify AI-provided legal sources.
agencies: Courts Administration Authority of South Australia
content: The information sheet accompanies the Generative AI Guidelines approved by the Judges of the Supreme Court of South Australia, adopted from 1 January 2026 and applying to the Supreme, District, Magistrates, Youth and Environment, Resources and Development Courts and the Court of Disputed Returns. It gives self-represented litigants additional guidance on two issues highlighted in those Guidelines: restrictions on uploading documents received in litigation into a Gen AI product, and the need to verify legal sources and references produced by Gen AI. It explains the Harman obligation, under which documents obtained through discovery, disclosure or subpoena may be used only for the proceeding, and notes other restrictions arising from confidentiality, privilege, suppression orders and copyright. Uploading such documents to open Gen AI systems such as the free version of ChatGPT risks their use in training or disclosure, and a breach of the Harman obligation may amount to contempt of court, exposing the litigant to a fine, custody, costs, compensation or other orders. Litigants should not upload documents from another party unless satisfied the system is closed and will not release or train on the material, and are given questions to ask about data use, retention, paid tiers and access. The sheet warns that Gen AI hallucinates cases, references, laws and section numbers, that litigants remain responsible for wrong information given to the court, and that AI output can never be treated as legal advice. It offers prompting tips, such as specifying the court, jurisdiction, year, case type and applicable rules (Uniform Civil Rules 2020, Joint Criminal Rules 2022 or Uniform Special Statutory Rules 2022), and directs litigants to AustLII, BarNet JADE, SA Legislation, the Law Handbook, the Courts Administration Authority website, the Legal Services Commission, the Law Society and JusticeNet SA for verification and help. It closes by describing what court staff can and cannot assist with.
aiSummary: South Australian courts advise self-represented litigants not to upload discovered, subpoenaed, privileged or suppressed documents to open generative AI tools, warn that doing so may be contempt of court, and require them to verify every AI-provided legal source before relying on it.

title: AI considerations within the Essentials
description: ASD guidance, published on 15 October 2026, on applying the ASD Essentials to artificial intelligence whether an organisation consumes, develops or deploys AI.
content: ASD published this as guidance on 15 October 2026. The publication page (https://www.cyber.gov.au/publication/ai-considerations-within-the-essentials) shows "Published 15 Oct 2026" and the PDF is at https://www.cyber.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/AI%20considerations%20within%20the%20Essentials.pdf. The page describes it as guidance that helps cyber security practitioners understand considerations for scoping, implementing and assessing controls in AI environments, especially within the enterprise IT chapter. ASD presents it as guidance. It uses 'should' language, and its disclaimer says it is 'of a general nature'. The same day's news item (https://www.cyber.gov.au/news/asd-essentials-evolving-our-approach-to-cyber-security-resilience) says ASD launched the ASD Essentials on 15 October 2026 as an evolution of the Essential Eight, in chapters for enterprise IT, operational technology and cloud, and that during the transition ASD keeps both frameworks on cyber.gov.au. It also says: "Until associated regulatory changes are communicated by regulators, organisations should continue to meet their current regulatory obligations." The publication says the Essentials framework applies whether an organisation consumes, develops or deploys AI. It covers AI assets in scoping (including models, training data, model artefacts and inference endpoints), prompt injection, the integrity and provenance of model weights and training data, least privilege for AI agents and integrations, AI agents' non-person identities, AI tools capable of administrative actions operating through privileged environments, and logging of prompts and outputs. ASD's transition guidance, also published on 15 October 2026 (https://www.cyber.gov.au/publication/transitioning-from-the-essential-eight), says the enterprise IT chapter's Governance and culture domain includes an artificial intelligence accountability principle, and that these governance areas were not assessed as part of the Essential Eight maturity model. The AI considerations PDF (p 5) ties executive AI accountability to the ISM principle. The record sits with ASD's other AI cyber security guidance: Careful adoption of agentic AI services (asd-careful-adoption-agentic-ai-services-2026), Agentic AI harnesses (asd-agentic-ai-harnesses-2026), the Blueprint for Secure Cloud artificial intelligence usage policy requirement (asd-blueprint-secure-cloud-ai-usage-policy) and Frontier AI models and their impact on cyber security (asd-frontier-ai-models-cyber-security-2026).

description: Tasmanian Government announcement that major AI and data-centre proponents will be expected to contribute to a Local Community Benefit Fund supporting host communities, alongside paying network costs and quarterly public reporting of water and energy use.
content: On 14 October 2026 the Premier of Tasmania announced that the Tasmanian Government will establish a Local Community Benefit Fund so communities hosting major AI and data-centre developments share directly in the benefits. The fund is to support local infrastructure, skills and training, community organisations and initiatives that improve liveability and economic participation in host communities. Major AI and data-centre proponents will be expected to: pay their own infrastructure and network costs; help grow Tasmania's energy supply by supporting new renewable generation and additional energy capacity; locate in appropriate industrial precincts away from urban areas; protect consumers so water and power demand does not compromise supply security or raise costs for other users; contribute to the Local Community Benefit Fund; and publicly report water and energy use each quarter. The announcement builds on the Government's draft Statement of Expectations for Data Centres and AI Infrastructure and reflects issues raised through the Parliamentary Inquiry into AI Data Centres. content: ASIC media release 26-226MR (https://www.asic.gov.au/about-asic/news-centre/find-a-media-release/2026-releases/26-226mr-asic-strengthens-ai-trading-safeguards-and-streamlines-market-integrity-rules) is dated 24 September 2026 on the page (displayDate). It announces amendments to the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) 2017 and the ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) 2017 that modernise trading-systems obligations for algorithmic trading, including AI and machine learning, require participants to test, monitor and govern trading systems and algorithms, align more closely with IOSCO principles, apply trading-system requirements consistently to manually entered and automated orders, and clarify the false or misleading appearance rule for AI-enabled and other trading. The release says the amendments follow Consultation Paper 386 and take effect in 2028 after an 18-month transition. The release does not mention a kill switch or a seven-year record-keeping period. ASIC consultation CS 63 (https://www.asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/consultations/cs-63-proposed-updates-to-rg-265-and-rg-266-and-withdrawal-of-rg-241) states Released 24 September 2026 and that comments close at 5 pm AEDT on 5 November 2026. It states that the market integrity rules were amended in September 2026 and that the rules commence on 18 March 2028 after an 18-month transition. It proposes updates to RG 265 and RG 266 and moving relevant guidance from RG 241 into those guides so RG 241 can be retired. The CS 63 page does not mention a kill switch or seven-year record keeping. Attachments 5 and 6, the marked-up compilations of the securities and futures rules, state that the changes are in force from 18 March 2028 and that market participants and market operators can continue to comply with the rules as in force on 15 October 2024 until 18 March 2028. The Federal Register of Legislation records ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Securities Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/574 (F2026L01223, https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L01223/latest/text) and ASIC Market Integrity Rules (Futures Markets) Amendment Instrument 2026/575 (F2026L01224, https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2026L01224/latest/text). Each instrument is dated 15 September 2026 and was registered on 17 September 2026. Section 2 of each instrument states that it commences on the day that is 18 months after the day it is registered. The instruments do not use the term kill switch. They do set seven-year record obligations in the amended trading-system rules. In the securities instrument, a trading participant must maintain records of trading messages identified under the monitoring and post-trade surveillance rule, and any measures taken, for seven years from the date of the relevant trading message (rule 5.6.3A(3)); maintain records that demonstrate compliance with the trading-algorithm controls and testing obligations for seven years (rule 5.6.3B(4)); and document and retain for at least seven years records of the methodology, scope and results of the Initial Certification Review (rule 5.6.4(4)), the Material Change Review (rule 5.6.8(4)) and the Annual Review (rule 5.6.8A(5)), and of recommended changes applied as a result. The futures instrument states the corresponding obligations in rules 2.2B.3(3), 2.2B.4(4), 2.2B.5(4), 2.2B.8(4) and 2.2B.9(5).
aiSummary: ASIC Market Integrity Rules amendments (F2026L01223, F2026L01224) for algorithmic and AI-enabled trading, made 15 September 2026. The Federal Register schedules them to start on 17 March 2028.

content: On 24 September 2026 the Prime Minister announced a Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (PM&C)-led rapid review of whether existing legislative, governance and information-sharing arrangements are fit for purpose to prepare for and respond to cyber incidents involving artificial intelligence. PM&C published formal terms of reference the same day (https://www.pmc.gov.au/resources/terms-reference-rapid-review-australian-government-arrangements-ai-driven-cyber-incident; release date Thursday 24 September 2026). The review page states that PM&C leads the review in collaboration with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia. Per the terms of reference, recommendations scope covers: reporting requirements relating to AI-driven cyber incidents, AI-identified cyber vulnerabilities and cyber-related AI safety incidents (including obligations, thresholds, pathways and systems); Commonwealth governance and information-sharing arrangements for managing incidents involving AI (including roles, responsibilities and escalation pathways); engagement and information-sharing obligations of AI firms (including notification requirements and cooperation arrangements during incidents); the adequacy of existing system and legislative, regulatory and enforcement frameworks in deterring AI-driven cyber incidents (including whether current offences, liabilities, penalties and enforcement mechanisms are sufficient and effective); and mechanisms to strengthen networks and systems of government departments and agencies against AI vulnerabilities. PM&C states the review will also inform Australia's AI Standards and international work on safety incident reporting. The Prime Minister's disclosure of the underlying OpenAI / Medicare statistics portal incident is recorded separately as timeline event tl-2026-09-24-pm-discloses-openai-medicare-portal-access. This record is the government rapid review with published terms of reference; it is not a completed instrument and it is not OpenAI's later company taskforce.

title: Australia's Fourth Open Government National Action Plan (NAP4) consultation
description: Attorney-General's Department public consultation on proposed commitments for Australia's Fourth Open Government Partnership National Action Plan (January 2027–December 2028), including DTA-led Proposed Commitment 5 on AI transparency and digital accessibility. Submissions close on 6 November 2026.
content: On 16 October 2026 the Attorney-General announced public consultation on Australia's Fourth Open Government Partnership National Action Plan (NAP4). The Attorney-General's Department consultation hub lists the consultation as opened on 15 October 2026 and closing on 6 November 2026. NAP4 would cover the two-year implementation period from January 2027 to December 2028. The consultation paper presents seven proposed commitments developed by the Open Government Forum; final commitments are subject to Forum agreement and government approval. Proposed Commitment 5, "Enhancing transparency of AI and digital accessibility", is led by the Digital Transformation Agency. It would use AI-enabled assessment tools for regular reviews of the quality, completeness and accessibility of agency AI Transparency Statements and of the digital experience of public-facing government information and services (accessibility, usability, discoverability and standards compliance). Findings would be published through a public benchmarking/insights program supporting DTA stewardship of Australian Government AI policy and the Digital Experience Policy. Proposed Commitment 1 (National Media Literacy Strategy, led by the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts) also names AI's effect on media literacy. Primary consultation page: https://consultations.ag.gov.au/integrity/ogp-fnap. Consultation paper: https://consultations.ag.gov.au/integrity/ogp-fnap/user_uploads/ogp-fnap_consultation-paper.pdf. Minister's media release (16 October 2026): https://ministers.ag.gov.au/media-centre/have-your-say-australias-next-open-government-national-action-plan-16-10-2026.

content: Circular to Practitioners No. 14 of 2026, dated 21 October 2026 and signed by Registrar Penelope Ikedife, publishes Guidelines for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence. The circular says the guidelines apply to all court users, including lawyers, litigants, witnesses and other third parties who produce documents to the Court, in all Supreme Court proceedings, and that they commence that day until further notice. The guidelines (as at 21 October 2026) say they apply when court users use generative AI to help create, write, edit, modify or otherwise prepare a document for court proceedings (para 2.1). Part 3 calls for caution with pleadings, written submissions, lists of documents and other documents (paras 3.2 to 3.4), and particular caution with affidavit materials, witness statements and other witness evidence (para 3.5). Expert reports must contain the expert’s own opinion and process of reasoning and comply with the relevant practice direction and Expert Witness Code of Conduct (para 3.6). Court users should not enter confidential, privileged or private information, including information subject to a suppression or non-publication order, into an AI tool that is not a closed tool (para 3.8). Any person who uses generative AI to prepare a document must verify all content before submitting it, and AI-generated content must be checked by a person, not solely by a generative AI tool (paras 4.1 and 4.3). Court users are not required to certify the use of generative AI, but must disclose that use if asked, and a person who uses it is expected to be able to explain the tool, how it was used, and the checks (paras 4.4 and 4.5). Inconsistent use may lead to less weight, a document being disregarded, adjournment, costs, or dismissal, and for lawyers a referral to the Legal Profession Board of Tasmania or personal costs orders (paras 5.1 and 5.2).
aiSummary: Supreme Court of Tasmania guidelines, commencing 21 October 2026, for all court users in all proceedings: verify generative AI documents, take particular care with pleadings and evidence, keep confidential material out of open tools, and disclose use if asked.
